content.title: About
content.content: Alfredo sauce with seafood is a creamy sauce made from heavy cream, Parmesan cheese, and butter, enriched with a selection of seafood such as shrimp, mussels, and calamari. It blends the smooth, buttery flavor of classic Alfredo with the briny taste of the sea, making it perfect for pasta, risotto, and baked dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original Alfredo sauce was created in the early 1900s at the restaurant "Alfredo" in Rome.
Traditional Italian Alfredo contains only butter, cream, and Parmesan, without any seafood.
Seafood is usually cooked separately and folded into the sauce at the end to preserve its tenderness.
The cream used is typically 30‑35% fat, giving the sauce its characteristic thick texture.
In the United States Alfredo is most often served with fettuccine, while in Italy it is paired with tagliatelle.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Seafood (shrimp, mussels, calamari) provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Seafood contains polyunsaturated omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart and vascular health.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cream and Parmesan add calcium and vitamin D, important for bone strength.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Seafood is rich in vitamin B12 and niacin, which aid nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Parmesan provides antioxidant compounds such as vitamin A and enzymes that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels, or calamari, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The creamy base is rich in saturated fats, so people with elevated cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Parmesan and added salt can increase sodium intake, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly stored seafood can harbor bacteria such as Salmonella, so proper refrigeration is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sauce hot over pasta (fettuccine, spaghetti), rice, or risotto, or use it as a base for a seafood casserole with vegetables. Warm the sauce gently, then stir in the cooked seafood at the end to keep it juicy. Garnish with fresh parsley or lemon zest for extra brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months after cooling completely. Reheat thoroughly before serving and avoid repeated heating cycles.
